newsitem.title: USA: Politicians care about kids - but how much?.
newsitem.headline: Politicians care about kids - but how much?.

text.p: Politicians have always kissed babies. This year they have started voting for them.
Mammoth budget bills moving through Congress expand health care to many of the 10 million uninsured U.S. children, grant a $500-per-child tax credit and create new college tax breaks.

The emphasis on the young and their stressed-out baby-boom parents is even more striking in the midst of politically charged votes to curtail Medicare benefits for the elderly. By wide margins the Senate last week did the unthinkable, voting to make affluent seniors pay higher Medicare premiums and gradually increase the eligibility age to 67 from 65.

That is a flip from 1996, when Congress reduced welfare benefits to children while protecting Medicare. Even if the changes do not become law, analysts call the effort a step toward altering the generational politics of Washington where aid to the elderly has been seen as sacrosanct while children's programmes sometimes went begging.
"Despite all the rhetoric about children we don't spend money on children," Michael Tanner, an analyst at the free-market Cato Institute, said.
Much of the federal budget is devoted to Medicare and Social Security. "That's where the money is, that's where the debate is and that's why we're cutting back," he said.
A study by the liberal Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities found spending on income maintenance programmes was ten times greater per elderly individual than per child.

"I don't think (lawmakers) want to take away from the elderly to give to the kids, I don't think it's that overt," the center's Wendell Primus said. "It's happening for other reasons. They have to get a handle on Medicare."
The Children's Defence Fund says looking just at federal spending gives an incomplete picture of society's support for children and warns against overplaying generational bias.
Changing spending patterns may be the easy part for Congress. Creating effective new programmes is harder.

Both political parties share a growing worry about long-term forecasts showing unsustainable growth in mandatory "entitlement" programmes like Medicare, where everyone who is eligible automatically receives benefits. The same fiscal pressures pushing lawmakers to rewrite the Medicare compact with seniors are making it tough to deliver new aid to children, especially health care.

Spooked by the notion of a new entitlement, Congress wants to make children's health insurance voluntary. Lawmakers are offering states enticing pots of money to design these insurance programmes but not requiring them to do so.

The $16 billion included in the budget bill was supposed to cover up to 5 million children over five years, but congressional auditors predict it will reach a fraction of that -- from 500,000 to about a million. That does not include an extra $8 billion passed by the Senate.

"The rhetoric has clearly outstripped what people are willing to do," said a congressional budget analyst who compared the debate to President Clinton's failed plan for universal health care. "Lawmakers objected to the Clinton plan because of the compulsory nature. Then when you didn't make it compulsory it was very hard to get the increases in coverage."
Governors and Republicans who designed the children's care bill vehemently disagree, saying the Congressional Budget Office wrongly assumes states will divert the federal money to other purposes.

Republicans say one of the biggest money grabs in recent years came when states learned how to milk an existing entitlement -- the Medicaid health programme for the poor. Charging that states took Medicaid money and "started buying sports stadiums," a Republican aide said the new plan had safeguards to prevent a recurrence.
Others say states are reeling under high Medicaid costs while millions of children eligible for the programme are not enrolled, disproving the notion that entitlements work.

Democrats attack the Republican plans but the two parties are not that far apart. From Clinton down, Democratic alternatives are voluntary. Many Democrats say it is possible to draw an effective programme by inducing states to expand Medicaid, not create new programmes.
